title: Security & Compliance: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, Secure SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence Workflows, and Risk Exceptions
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's operational controls and workflows for: RBAC & authentication, audit logging, data residency & retention, secure SDLC controls, incident response security procedures, compliance evidence collection, and risk/exception handling. It is intended for service owners, platform engineers, security reviewers, and compliance auditors.

Key contacts and owners
- Security (policy & evidence lead): Aisha Patel (security)
- Identity & Access control owner: Eng-SRE (team alias: eng-sre-iam)
- Logging & Observability owner: Eng-Platform (team alias: eng-platform-obs)
- Data residency and retention owner: Eng-Infra (eng-infra-data)
- Secure SDLC owner: Eng-Developer-Experience (eng-devx-sec)
- Compliance approver / Risk Committee: Security Governance Committee (sec-gov@redwood.com)

1) RBAC & Authentication

Purpose
- Provide least-privilege access to production and sensitive systems while enabling developer productivity and safe on-call operations.

Principles
- Least privilege by default.
- Role-based assignments; temporary elevation for on-call or emergency tasks.
- Credential hygiene: no long-lived user API keys for human users in production.
- Periodic access reviews and automated attestations.

Roles and role mappings (examples)
- role:platform-readonly -> groups:observability, auditors
- role:platform-operator -> groups:eng-sre, eng-platform
- role:customer-support-limited -> groups:customer-success (no access to PII or customer-resident data)

Authentication methods
- SSO (OIDC) via our IdP (Okta). All human users authenticate via SSO and MFA (required: TOTP + hardware key recommended).
- Service-to-service via short-lived workload identities (K8s service accounts with Workload Identity or cloud-native IAM roles).
- Machine credentials: only issued via automation (Vault-issued dynamic credentials).

Policy lifecycle and controls
1. Policy author creates/updates IaC policy (terraform/iam-templates) in private git repo: infra/iam-policies.
2. Change requires CODEOWNERS approval from eng-sre-iam and one security reviewer.
3. Automated policy linting and simulation tests run in CI; PR blocking tests prevent granting overly-broad permissions.
4. Deployment is gated and logged; policy change rollout tracked in the policy-change dashboard.

Access review cadence
- Quarterly automated attestation for all privileged groups (eng-sre, eng-platform, customer-success-elevated).
- Monthly privileged session audit for accounts that used privilege elevation.

Emergency access (break glass)
- Break-glass requests must be raised via PagerDuty incident and require: incident id, justification, duration (max 6 hours). All break-glass events generate an immediate audit entry and post-incident review.

2) Audit logging

Objectives
- Ensure reproducible audit trails for access, configuration changes, and data exfiltration-relevant events.
- Provide evidence for compliance audits and investigations.

What to log (minimum required fields)
- Authentication events: user/service id, method, timestamp, source IP, MFA status.
- Authorization decisions: policy id, evaluated principals, resource id, outcome (allow/deny).
- Admin/config changes: author, change diff, service, rollout id.
- Data access events: dataset id, subject (user/service), operation (read/write/export), affected rows/objects (summary), timestamp.
- Code deployment events: commit id, deploy job id, target cluster/region, deploy actor.

Logging infrastructure and tiers
- Real-time streaming: logs forwarded to centralized pipeline (Kafka -> Splunk/Datadog). Critical security and infra logs are ingested with high priority.
- Hot retention: 13 months (searchable).
- Cold archive: 7 years (S3 Glacier or equivalent) for compliance-bound customers and selected audit categories.
- Integrity: write-once append model, immutability for archived buckets, and quarterly checksums.

Log access and protection
- Access to raw logs restricted by roles: sec-audit-read, eng-platform-obs.
- Anonymization: PII is redacted at the producer when possible; sensitive fields are tokenized or encrypted in transit and at rest.

Alerting and retention SLOs
- Delivery SLO: 99.9% of critical audit events delivered to the pipeline within 60s.
- Retention SLO: Hot logs retained and queryable for 13 months with 95% read availability.

3) Data residency and retention

Customer options and defaults
- Customers can pin data residency to supported regions: us-east1, us-west1, eu-west1, asia-southeast1.
- Default for unpinned tenants: multi-region with primary in us-east1 (for historic customers) unless contractually specified.

Storage classes and retention schedule
| Data class | Example | Hot retention | Cold archive | Owner |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Audit logs (critical) | Auth events, admin changes | 13 months | 7 years | eng-platform-obs |
| Customer request logs (pseudonymized) | API call traces | 90 days | 2 years | eng-serving-runtime |
| Customer data (customer-controlled) | Model inputs/outputs if customer chooses residency | Configured per contract | Per contract | customer-data-owner |
| Backups (infra) | DB snapshots | 30 days | 1 year | eng-infra |

Retention rules and deletion
- Retention is enforced by lifecycle policies. Deletion is automated except where legal hold exists.
- Legal hold: compliance or legal can place a hold; only Security Governance Committee or legal may release hold.

Data residency enforcement
- Control plane metadata may be global; customer content, KV caches, and persistence layers are pinned per tenancy when configured.
- Network controls: VPC peering/private gateway options for Private deployments; egress controls enforced at host-level and cloud routing.

4) Secure SDLC (security controls integrated into development lifecycle)

Gates and controls
- Threat modeling: required for all services exposing external or customer-data plane interfaces. Template stored at /confluence/eng-developer-experience/threat-model-template.
- Code scanning: SAST and dependency SCA run on every PR; high/critical findings block merge.
- Secret scanning: pre-commit hooks and CI checks; any detected secret triggers automated rotation workflow.
- Infrastructure as Code review: terraform plan outputs and drift checks required; policy-as-code (OPA/rego) checks enforced in CI.
- Deployment approvals: production deploys require a successful pipeline, passing security checks, and at least one approver from the owning team plus one security reviewer for high-impact changes.

Developer responsibilities
- Add unit and integration tests for security-sensitive logic.
- Keep third-party dependencies updated; respond to security advisory tickets within SLA.

SLA for security fixes
- Critical (RCE, data exfil): fix or mitigation within 72 hours.
- High (auth bypass, privilege escalation): fix or mitigation within 7 days.
- Medium/low: triage and schedule per roadmap.

5) Incident response security procedures

Purpose
- Provide a consistent playbook for security incidents impacting confidentiality, integrity, or availability of Redwood services or customer data.

Severity classification
- Sev1 (critical): ongoing data exfiltration, production-wide outage, or confirmed compromise of key material.
- Sev2 (high): service degradation affecting multiple customers or confirmed exploit with limited scope.
- Sev3 (medium): single-customer impact or contained security bug.

Initial triage & containment (steps)
1. Detection: alert fired via IDS/monitoring or customer report; on-call notifies Security Incident Lead (SIL).
2. Triage: SIL evaluates scope, assigns severity, and notifies Incident Response channel.
3. Containment: implement network isolation, rotate compromised keys, and enable enhanced logging.
4. Evidence preservation: snapshot affected hosts, capture memory if required, and lock relevant logs to immutable archive.
5. Communicate: use pre-approved templates for customer and internal comms; legal and communications teams joined for Sev1.

Forensics and evidence handling
- Evidence chain-of-custody must be recorded for all collected artifacts.
- Forensic images stored in secure archive with restricted access and logged access.
- Logs relevant to the investigation are copied to an immutable store and a hash recorded.

Post-incident activities
- Postmortem published within 7 business days for Sev1/Sev2 and 15 business days for Sev3, including root cause, remediation, timeline, and preventive actions.
- Action items assigned with owners and due dates; security validates closure.

6) Compliance evidence workflows

Evidence catalogue (examples)
- Identity & Access: CODEOWNERS, IAM policy git history, quarterly attestation reports.
- Logging: retention config, delivery SLO dashboards, archival checksums.
- SDLC: PR lists for critical deploys, SAST reports, threat model artifacts.
- Data residency: contract clauses, tenant residency flags, encryption keys KMS logs.

Evidence collection process
1. Owner identifies evidence artifacts required by control mapping (SOC2/ISO/GDPR).
2. Evidence artifact stored in the compliance evidence repo (immutable) with metadata: artifact id, control id, owner, retention date.
3. Periodic validation job verifies artifact freshness and integrity; failures create remediation tickets assigned to owners.

Audit readiness and requests
- Audit playbook: The compliance team coordinates auditor access, scoping, and pre-audit checklist.
- Temporary read-only access to evidence artifacts is granted to auditors with time-limited credentials. All auditor activity logged.

7) Risk and exceptions

Exception request process (numbered)
1. Submit exception request via the Risk & Exceptions template in the compliance portal (fields: control impacted, justification, compensating controls, duration, owner).
2. Security reviewer performs technical assessment and suggests compensating controls (e.g., enhanced logging, limited-user whitelist, shorter TTLs).
3. Risk Committee reviews and either approves, approves with conditions, or denies.
4. Approved exceptions are timeboxed (max 90 days) unless renewed via the same flow; renewals require fresh justification and evidence of compensating control effectiveness.

Exception decision template (table)
| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Requester | engineering-service-owner |
| Control impacted | e.g., RBAC: privilege elevation flow |
| Compensating controls | e.g., enhanced audit logging, session timeout 15m |
| Approval | Security Governance Committee |
| Expiry | 2027-05-15 |

Monitoring exceptions
- All approved exceptions are listed in the exceptions registry and reviewed monthly. Any sign of misuse triggers immediate revocation.
